1:
The opening sentence is textually unsettled and the two who notice it say so. Clarke reports several readings, too minute to set out, whose effect is that if it be expedient to glory, which does not become him, he will proceed to visions. Ellicott judges the best-attested text to be one that would run in English as I must needs glory; it is not, indeed, expedient, but I will come, and reads the sequence of thought as mingled feelings, the writer constrained by his opponents' taunts into what looked like self-assertion while conscious that it was not in the highest sense expedient. Chrysostom asks why it should be inexpedient at all, since a man knows his own revelations whether he speaks of them or not, and answers that knowing them ourselves does not lift us up so much as publishing them to others, since it is not the nature of good deeds to exalt a man but their being witnessed to and known. Calvin reads the restraint as a rebuke of the rivals, since it was a shame that they should scrape commendations together from every quarter to put themselves on a level with so distinguished a man; and he warns that the more numerous a man's graces the less he ought to think of his own excellence, such a thought being a labyrinth in which one is dazzled while remaining ignorant of himself.

Why the account is given in the third person is explained the same way by two of them. Barnes suggests it was because the writer had been accused of boasting and had just admitted that glorying did not become him, so that although he could not boast directly he could tell of a man about whom there would be no impropriety in boasting; and he notes that speaking of oneself so is not uncommon, instancing Caesar's practice and the fourth evangelist's way of referring to himself. Calvin gives the same reason in the writer's own voice: I should have preferred to be silent and keep the whole matter suppressed, but these obstinate persons will not allow me, and so I shall mention it as it were in a stammering way, that it may be seen I speak through constraint. On the dating, Clarke and Ellicott independently reckon back from a letter of about the year fifty-seven and arrive at forty-three, Clarke placing it near the journey from Tarsus to Antioch, and Ellicott in the unrecorded activity before the arrival there, where such an encouragement would have been unspeakably precious. Ellicott considers and sets aside the trance in the temple.

Whether one rapture is described or two divides them squarely. Clarke says we cannot absolutely tell whether the third heaven and paradise are the same place, thinks they probably are not, and concludes it likely there were at least two raptures. Ellicott agrees the stress laid on the second hinders us from thinking it identical with the first, and offers the nearest distinction he can, that the first revealed the glory of the throne as Moses and Isaiah and Ezekiel saw it while the second brought before the spirit the peace ineffable; speculation about which lies nearer the earth he calls idle. Robertson takes the opposite view, that paradise is apparently used as the equivalent of the third heaven, notes that some Jewish writers place paradise in the third heaven while the rabbis variously reckoned two heavens, three, or seven, and cautions against committing the apostle to any celestial gradation. On the word itself Barnes traces it from eastern Asia into Greek and the western languages, giving the Sanskrit sense of a cultivated upland, the Armenian of a garden about a house, and the Persian of the walled pleasure-parks of princes; the edition of Calvin reproduces that etymology verbatim.
5:
Whether the phrase points to a person or to a thing is the first question, and Barnes reports both before choosing. Some, he says, take the words to mean of such a thing or of such a transaction, so that the sense would be that the writer may justly boast of being caught up to heaven as of an event whose whole glory belongs to the one who exalted him, while of himself he will not boast; Barnes names two who explain it so and rejects them, holding that the connexion requires a person and that the passage is partly ironical, the writer keeping himself directly out of view and saying only that of such a man they would admit it proper to boast. Gill describes the same manoeuvre as a distinguishing of himself from himself, himself in paradise from himself on earth, so that though he might lawfully glory of a person so exalted he chose to forbear because the case was his own. Clarke says bluntly that modesty alone prevents the naming, since the account can be understood of no one else and would otherwise be wholly irrelevant. Robertson puts it as though there were two Pauls, and adds that in a sense there were.

Ellicott turns that division of the self into a meditation of his own. There is, if we rightly understand it, an almost exquisite sadness in the distinction drawn between the old self of fourteen years ago with its abundance of revelations and the new self of the present, feebler and sadder, worn with cares and sorrows and the daily rush of life; then he saw with open vision, now he walks by faith and not by the thing seen, and can hardly recognise his own identity, speaking of the man who once had that capacity for the beatific vision as though he were another and almost as if he were dead and gone. Ellicott generalises the experience and then withdraws the generalisation: the complaint of being no longer what one was takes manifold forms, the soldier recalling the stir and rush of battle, the poet finding the vision and the faculty divine no longer entrusted to his keeping, the orator who once wielded a fierce democracy at will complaining now of a stammering tongue; but this case has a sadness peculiar to itself, since faith and hope and love and peace remain while a glory has passed away from the earth.

On the disclaimer that follows, Barnes takes the sentence as a serious statement made after the irony rather than a continuation of it: if the writer chose to boast as others did he would have ample material and would not be boasting emptily, since he could urge claims that anyone would admit well-founded. Ellicott reads it in the same direction but keys it to the vocabulary of madness which he finds dominant in the words for fool and folly throughout the passage, so that the sense is, if I should boast of that I shall not be acting as a madman does, for I will confine myself to a simple statement of fact. Robertson notices the apparent contradiction with an earlier chapter where the writer had called himself a fool, and resolves it by observing that the speaker here is the Paul who was caught up, supposing he were to tell what he heard. Clarke draws the practical moral out of the abrupt breaking-off, asking who that had received such honour would have kept silence about it for fourteen years, and observing that the revelations were mentioned for two opposite reasons, lest enemies think meanly of him and, having said that much, lest friends think too highly; it is a rare gift, he adds, to discern when to speak and when to be silent.
7:
Ellicott begins with the word rather than the conjectures, and the word turns out to be sharper than the English suggests. The Greek would better be rendered stake: it is used of the stakes driven in to form a palisade round a grave, as in the Iliad where they dig a trench full deep and fix their stakes about it, and a sharp-pointed stake of that kind was the instrument of impaling, the Greek verbs for impaling and crucifying being almost interchangeable, so that Euripides can ask whether to hurl the captives from a rock or fix their bodies on the stake. Ellicott adds the telling detail that opponents of the faith like Celsus and Lucian preferred the word stake to cross as the more ignominious, and spoke of Jesus as having been impaled. Clarke reaches the same sense by another route, noting that the noun means a stake and the cognate verb to be tied to one by way of punishment, and that the word is used of the most oppressive afflictions; he insists that whatever it was it was outward, since it was neither sin nor sinfulness, sin having never had and never being able to have the tendency to keep a man from being exalted.

On what the thorn actually was the reports conflict, including about who held what. Clarke lists the older conjectures and assigns them: earache to Tertullian, headache to Chrysostom, and many grievous bodily torments to Cyprian; his own view is that the reference is simply to the distresses endured through the opposition at Corinth. Calvin reports the headache view without naming its author and says instead that Chrysostom inclined to refer the thorn to Hymeneus and Alexander and men like them, who under the devil's instigation gave much annoyance. Calvin's own reading is broader and turns on a definition: under the term is comprehended every kind of temptation with which the apostle was exercised, and flesh here denotes not the body but that part of the soul which has not yet been regenerated. He is emphatic in rejecting one reading in particular, that those act a ridiculous part who think the temptation was to lust, a fancy which must be repudiated and put far away. Barnes leaves the identification aside and dwells on the stated purpose, arguing that the man was naturally proud, self-confident and eminently ambitious, so that pride would be his besetting sin after conversion, and that if such a measure was needed to keep him humble no one else should be surprised to need one.

That the prayer was addressed to Christ is pressed by two of them as doctrine. Barnes argues it from the following verse and notes that even Rosenmuller maintained it and that the Socinians themselves admit it, drawing the conclusion that it is right to go to Christ in trouble and right to worship him, prayer being the most solemn act of adoration. Clarke puts the same argument more compactly and calls it a sure proof of divinity, since only an omniscient being can be made an object of prayer. On the number, Clarke suggests either that three stands for an indefinite many or, more likely, that three solemn and fixed applications are meant, and both he and Ellicott hear behind them the threefold prayer in Gethsemane, where likewise the answer was not compliance but strength to endure. Ellicott reports that some of the better manuscripts omit the possessive in the reply, so that it becomes a general axiom that might is perfected in weakness, and regrets that the received rendering conceals the identity of that word with the one translated infirmity just after. Robertson makes the same point grammatically, that the verb is linear so power is continually increased as the weakness grows, and Clarke glosses the resting of the power as overshadowing like a tent.
11:
Chrysostom notices that the self-accusation has hardened as the passage went on. At the outset the writer had asked to be received as foolish and had spoken as in foolishness, but now, dropping the qualifying particle, he calls himself foolish outright; and having made his point he grapples unsparingly with the whole failing, teaching that none should praise himself where there is no necessity, since even where a reason existed this man called himself a fool for doing it. Chrysostom then observes where the blame is laid, not on the false apostles but wholly on the disciples, since it was they who compelled him. Calvin marks the same turn as a change of posture: having until now solicited their forgiveness by various apologies for a thing contrary to his own custom and to what was due his office, he stops soliciting and upbraids, throwing the blame on the Corinthians who ought to have been the first to discharge the office of praising him and to have set themselves vigorously against the calumniators. Henry states the duty plainly, that they had not stood up in his defence as they ought and so made it the more needful for him to insist on his own vindication. Robertson explains the unfulfilled obligation in the tense, that he means he ought now to be commended by them instead of having to glorify himself.

Ellicott hears the whole closing section as an echo of the storm just passed. The passage reproduces in compressed form most of the earlier topics, each with its characteristic phrase, so that the violence is over but the sky is not yet clear and we still hear the mutterings of receding thunder: he remembers again that he has been called insane, taunted with commending himself, treated as nothing beside those rivals who set themselves up as apostles extraordinary. Ellicott also reports that the two words for glorying are wanting in the better manuscripts, so the verse opens with a thrilling abruptness, I am become insane, it was you who compelled me. On the signs that follow, he notes the word is used first in the general sense of tokens and then specifically of works of supernatural power, and marks the passage as one where the apostle distinctly claims such power for himself and appeals to its exercise. Robertson counts the three separate words for miracle standing together. Calvin takes the patience differently from the others, referring it either to the writer's remaining invincible under every assault or, more probably, to his enduring injuries in silence and overcoming indignities by patience, since such heroic virtue is itself a kind of heavenly seal.

The closing verse is read by all of them as irony, and Barnes measures it against the orators. It contains a striking mixture of sarcasm and irony not exceeded, on one authority he cites, by any example in Demosthenes; and he paraphrases the sting: you have had the fullest proofs of my commission and are inferior to other churches in one respect only, that you were never burdened with the privilege of supporting me, and for that wrong I ask your pardon. Ellicott traces the insinuation being answered, that he cared less for them than for the Macedonian churches because he had kept his independence and taken no gifts, and notes that the word for being burdensome is the same characteristic term for sponging which his rivals had evidently used of him, so that he dwells on it with a touch of irony. Robertson calls it consummate irony directed at the stingy element in the church. Calvin turns it into a charge of double ingratitude, since they had not only held in contempt the man whose kindness had put them under obligation but had turned his very generosity into an occasion of reproach, which he calls not merely insulting his modesty but cruelty.
14:
How many visits are being counted is settled the same way by three of them. Barnes says the writer does not mean he had been with them twice already but that he had twice before formed and been disappointed of the purpose, having intended to call both on the way to Macedonia and on the return; Clarke gives the same account and notes he now had more probability of going than before. Ellicott counts differently, reckoning the long first sojourn as the first occasion, the projected journey from Ephesus as the second, and the present preparation as the third. Robertson infers from the phrasing that there had in fact been only one visit so far, and observes that the verb for being burdensome now appears for the third time in the letter, so that they need not be apprehensive: he will be as financially independent of them as before. On the motive Calvin gives two reasons for the refusal of support, that he sought not their wealth and that he wished to act a father's part, and draws the pastoral rule while immediately guarding it, that a genuine pastor seeks not gain from his sheep but their welfare, though ministers are not to seek men with a view to having disciples of their own.

On the spending and being spent the commentators dwell on the second verb. Ellicott notes it implies spending to the last farthing, so that as he sought not theirs but them he is ready to spend for them not only all he has but even, as if to the verge of exhaustion, all that he is; Robertson gives the pair as an active and a passive, the second a late compound meaning to spend out utterly. Both find the same painful undertone in what follows, Ellicott speaking of an intense craving for affection to which it seemed their love varied inversely with his own. Clarke turns that into an observation from ordinary life, that it frequently happens to loving fathers that their disobedient children love them less in proportion as their own love increases, and that the most disobedient child is often the one on which the parents' tenderness is especially placed, as the shepherd feels more for the lost sheep than for the ninety-nine. Calvin calls the readiness to lay out not merely his endeavours but life itself an evidence of more than fatherly affection, and observes that he continues to cherish it while regarded with coldness, asking what heart though hard as iron such ardour would not soften; he adds that this is set down not for admiration but for imitation.

Whose words the confession of craft is has been disputed, and Clarke states the stakes bluntly. Many suppose the phrase about being crafty and catching them with guile is the apostle's own, and have concluded from it that guile and deceit are lawful in service of a religious purpose; that doctrine, Clarke says, is abominable, and the words are most evidently those of his detractors, against which he defends himself in the verses following. Barnes gives two reasons for the same conclusion, that it cannot be supposed a serious admission of having caught them by fraud, and that the objection is answered in the next verse. Ellicott reconstructs the sneer in the objectors' voice, granting that he made no demands on their purses in person but asking what to think of the collection for the saints and whose pockets it will reach, since they know him subtle enough to take them in somehow. Robertson notes that the word for crafty is quoted from the enemies and that a modern translator has done well to put the charges in quotation marks. Chrysostom accounts for the obscurity of the sentence by its subject, since where money and a defence about money are concerned it is reasonable that the words be wrapped in obscurity.
19:
A single letter decides how the section opens, and two of them adopt the same reading. Ellicott reports that many of the best manuscripts give the word for long ago rather than the word for again, in which case the sentence is better taken as an assertion than a question: you are thinking, and have been thinking for a long time, that it is to you we have been making our defence. Robertson renders it the same way as a progressive present, for a long time ye have been thinking. Both then insist on what is being denied. Ellicott notes the Greek verb is the one always used of a formal vindication, and says the writer deprecates the idea that he wishes to enter on such a thing at all, being anxious to explain his conduct but refusing to acknowledge that he stands at the bar of their judgment-seat; Robertson puts it that he is not just apologising but is in deadly earnest, as they will find out when he comes. Barnes and Clarke both stress the appeal that follows, Barnes calling it the solemn appeal of a Christian to God for the truth of what he says, and Clarke reading it as a denial that any sinister or unworthy motive lay behind the sending of Titus.

Calvin explains how a man's own vindication can be said to serve his readers' edification. Because he had been brought into contempt, many grew wanton as with loosened reins, so that respect for him would have been a means of leading them to repentance, since then they would have listened to his admonitions; and Calvin adds that it is a fault in Christ's servants to be too much concerned about their own reputation, which is why the writer declares in the first place that he speaks in God's presence and in the second that he has more concern for them than for himself. On the fear expressed next, Calvin finds it a token not merely of love but of indulgence to shun severity and reach for milder measures, paraphrasing the motive: I strive now to maintain my authority so that I may not be constrained to punish your obstinacy more severely when I come. Clarke reads the tense differently and thinks the present here stands for the past, so that the verse explains why he had not come before and had sent Titus instead, being unwilling to use the rod; on that reading, he says, all difficulty vanishes, whereas otherwise the statement seems to contradict what was said earlier in the letter.

The list of disorders draws Ellicott's closest work. He sets it against the catalogue of the fruits of repentance earlier in the letter and calls it a suggestive parallelism of contrast, the same keen perception of the shades of human character dwelling now on the manifold forms of opposition; and he goes through the words correcting the received renderings, noting that debates should rather be strifes or quarrels and that the English word carried a darker shade in older usage, when men could speak of a deadly debate between friends and a translator of Homer could make Achilles complain of debates past end. Robertson adds that the word for whisperings is onomatopoeic, formed from the verb to whisper into the ear and imitating the sibilant murmur of a snake charmer, and remarks of the word for backbitings that one could wish it existed nowhere else. On the closing verse Ellicott recovers a connection the English loses, that the verb for humbling reproduces the word already prominent in the letter and rendered variously as cast down, base and abasing, so that there is something almost plaintive in speaking of his disciples' sin as the only real humiliation he has to fear. Barnes observes that inflicting discipline punishes the one who inflicts it.
